title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
gist: Op-ed by Center for Democracy & Technology researchers argues social media age bans are easily circumvented (four in five Australian under-16s reached barred platforms), and that tightening enforcement would push kids to riskier corners of the web and degrade privacy for all. They urge limits on company data collection and user-controlled filtering tools instead.

themes.theme: State of age-ban legislation and evidence

insights.claim: France joined Australia in July in barring under-15s from major platforms before the country's top court blocked the ban on human rights grounds, the UK aims to bar under-16s in early 2027, and the EU has announced a plan to prohibit social media for under-15s.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Regulatory momentum for youth bans is broad but legally contestable; watch court challenges and compliance costs for platforms.

insights.claim: A study published this year found four in five Australian teens under 16 got onto barred platforms, using tactics such as a sibling's face for ID or drawn-on fake facial hair.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Weak enforceability undermines the premise of ban-driven user-loss risk for platforms.

insights.claim: Preliminary research after Australia's ban shows kids' screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected to spaces unmonitored and unknown to parents.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Displacement rather than reduction suggests engagement may migrate to smaller, less-moderated platforms.
insights.locator: A less safe internet for kids

themes.theme: Why circumvention is framed as a signal

insights.claim: The authors argue circumvention signals the limits of bans rather than a nuisance to deter, and that closing loopholes could push kids toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: A counter-consensus stance to pro-enforcement advocates, relevant to how regulators may calibrate enforcement.
insights.quote: circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred

insights.claim: Parents often help children lie to gain access to gated services, with research from 2011 showing parents taught children to evade Facebook age limits, because many believe the benefits of responsible access outweigh the risks.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Parental complicity lowers the effectiveness of age gates that rely on household compliance.
insights.locator: A less safe internet for kids

insights.claim: The most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street, and outdated, dying or under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Ban-driven migration could shift risk and trust-and-safety burden to smaller platforms.
insights.quote: the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street
insights.locator: A less safe internet for kids

themes.theme: Privacy and security costs of age verification

insights.claim: Age verification via profiling or document upload raises risks of data misuse, leaks and identity theft; Discord reported last year that third-party age-confirmation service 5CA was compromised, exposing at least 70,000 government ID images.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Age-assurance vendors are a concentrated breach and liability risk; expect scrutiny of that supply chain.
insights.locator: A less safe internet for all

insights.claim: Policymakers' attempts to curb workarounds have targeted VPNs, with state age-verification bills in Michigan and Utah (Utah's now blocked by a federal court) and Australia's eSafety Commissioner nudging platforms to detect and block VPN use.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Regulatory spillover into VPNs is a risk factor for privacy-tool providers and a litigation flashpoint.
insights.locator: A less safe internet for all

insights.claim: Requiring adult users to prove their age to access a VPN defeats its purpose and endangers journalists and human rights defenders with surveillance and retaliation risk.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Identity-linked VPN access would undercut the privacy-tool market's core value proposition.
insights.locator: A less safe internet for all

insights.claim: The authors recommend policymakers target company incentives by limiting data collection and use for targeting content, which would reduce unhealthy engagement; they say nearly all parents and teens they spoke with want such restrictions.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Data-minimisation rules would hit engagement-driven ad models more directly than age bans.

insights.claim: User-controlled tools such as keyword-based content filtering give families flexible control that platforms and policy cannot anticipate, for example blocking a nickname used to target a student.
insights.speaker: Michal Luria
insights.so_what: Product opportunity for granular, user-side moderation controls.
